explanations.explanation: Nahum calls Nineveh, the great city of Assyria, "…full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey." Three phrases in one breath, and none of them are flattering. You read that and know right away this is not a city you'd want to be left alone in.

Nahum's list doesn't have a single song in it. He says the city is "…full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey." Songs and dancing sound like an invitation to a party, and this is a woe, friend. Wrong guest list entirely.
Peace and rest never make Nahum's list. After calling Nineveh the city of blood, he says it's "…full of lies, full of plunder, never without prey." I'd skip the brochure and read the prophet.

Yes, Nahum moves from the "Charging horseman, flashing sword, shining spear…" straight to "heaps of slain, mounds of corpses, dead bodies without end…" This is a heavy part of the passage. I think this one hurts.

The text says otherwise. Right after the charging horseman, the flashing sword and the shining spear, Nahum describes "heaps of slain, mounds of corpses…" This is a heavy part of the passage. The picture of battle leads straight to its cost.
That's the word. Nahum says she "…betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft." Betrayal is the whole charge here. She is doing this to the very ones she deals with.
Not quite, friend. Nahum says she "…betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft." Blessing is the opposite of what the verse says. Betrayal is the charge.
Nahum says the opposite. She "…betrays nations by her prostitution and clans by her witchcraft." Nobody gets rescued in this verse. The nations and clans are the ones being let down.
That's it. "Behold, I am against you…" declares the LORD of Hosts. Notice how plain and short that is. Everything that follows in this passage comes after those words.
The LORD of Hosts says the opposite. His words are, "Behold, I am against you…" Nineveh doesn't get Him standing beside her in this verse.
Close in sound, far apart in meaning. The LORD of Hosts declares, "Behold, I am against you…" He is not on Nineveh's side here, and He says so directly.
The LORD says, "I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms." The audience is wide, not just the neighbors. Everyone watching sees it, and that is the point of the line.
The text goes much wider than that. The LORD says, "I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms." It's the nations and the kingdoms, not just her own people.

explanations.answer: Her king and no one else
explanations.explanation: Not just the king, friend. The LORD says, "I will show your nakedness to the nations and your shame to the kingdoms." The audience the verse names is the nations and the kingdoms, a lot bigger than one man.

Right. All who see her "…will recoil from you and say, ‘Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?’…" Then the LORD asks, "Where can I find comforters for you?" Two questions, and the verse leaves them as questions.
The word isn't fight. The people who see her say, "Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?" The question is about grieving, not fighting.
Nobody is talking about money here. The people who see her say, "Nineveh is devastated; who will grieve for her?" Grieving is the question. The bill never comes up.
Yes. Nahum says, "Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength…" Thebes was a city by the Nile, and she had real backing. That makes her story hit harder.
Edom and Moab aren't named in this verse at all. Nahum says, "Cush and Egypt were her boundless strength; Put and Libya were her allies." Those are the names to hold on to.
Persia and Media don't show up in this verse. Nahum names "Cush and Egypt…" as her boundless strength, with Put and Libya as allies. That's the crowd standing behind Thebes.
I can see why you'd think so, with all that water and all those allies. But Nahum says, "Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity." Thebes was taken, and Nahum doesn't soften it.
Right. Nahum says, "Yet she became an exile; she went into captivity." The water and the allies are named, and still that is what he says. Nahum tells it plainly.

Yes. Nahum says, "They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains." Casting lots is how the enemy settled who got which person. The text doesn't say more than that, so I won't either.
The text doesn't say they voted. Nahum says, "They cast lots for her dignitaries…" Lots, not ballots. Nobody in this verse is counting hands.
Swords aren't how Nahum says they decided. He says, "They cast lots for her dignitaries, and all her nobles were bound in chains." The lots did the deciding, and the nobles ended up in chains.

explanations.answer: Strong walls and allies didn't save her
explanations.explanation: That's the point, friend. Nahum asks Nineveh, "Are you better than Thebes…" Thebes had the Nile around her and Cush, Egypt, Put and Libya behind her, and she still went into captivity. If it happened to her, Nineveh shouldn't count on her own strength.
The text never says that. Nahum describes Thebes by the Nile with water around her and allies at her side, then says she went into captivity. He brings her up as a warning to Nineveh.

explanations.answer: Thebes promised to send Nineveh help
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the passage says Thebes promised help. Nahum points to Thebes as a city that was taken, even with her wall of water and her allies. She is the example, not the rescue.
Yes. Nahum says, "You too will become drunk; you will go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy." The city that was so loud earlier is looking for a place to hide. That's quite a change.
Revenge isn't in the verse. Nahum says Nineveh will "…go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy." The word is refuge, a place to get away to.
Treasure doesn't come up here. Nahum says she will "…go into hiding and seek refuge from the enemy." The word is refuge, a place to get away to.

explanations.answer: The figs fall into the eater's mouth
explanations.explanation: That's the picture. Nahum says, "All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs; when shaken, they fall into the mouth of the eater!" Shake the tree and the figs fall. That's how he pictures her fortresses.

explanations.answer: The figs hold tight to the branches
explanations.explanation: Nahum says the opposite. When the fig trees are shaken, the figs "…fall into the mouth of the eater!" The fortresses don't hold on at all.

explanations.answer: The trees put down deeper roots
explanations.explanation: The trees don't dig in. Nahum says that when they are shaken, the figs "…fall into the mouth of the eater!" It's a picture of fortresses that give up easily, nothing about roots.
Yes. Nahum says, "The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars." Gates are supposed to keep people out. These are wide open.
The text says the opposite. Nahum says, "The gates of your land are wide open to your enemies; fire consumes their bars." Not closed, wide open, and fire has consumed the bars.

Yes. After telling her to strengthen her fortresses, Nahum says, "There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down…" All that brick work and she still ends up there. Strengthening doesn't change what's coming.
Nahum says the opposite. Right after the order to "strengthen your fortresses." he says, "There the fire will devour you…" The walls aren't going to be her protection.
Nahum never says the enemy turns around. He says, "There the fire will devour you; the sword will cut you down…" All that repair work doesn't send anybody home.
That's the word. Nahum says, "The young locust strips the land and flies away." Strips is what the locust does, and then it flies away.
Locusts don't water anything, friend. Nahum says, "The young locust strips the land and flies away." It takes, it doesn't give.
Plowing is what a farmer does. Nahum says, "The young locust strips the land and flies away." Strips is the word, and then it's gone.

Yes. Nahum says the locusts "…settle on the walls on a cold day. When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where." He pictures her scribes the same way. They look settled until the sun comes up.
Nahum doesn't say they eat the walls. He says they settle on them on a cold day, and "When the sun rises, they fly away…" What happens at sunrise is that they fly away.
There's no doubling here. Nahum says, "When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where." The crowd doesn't grow, it disappears.
Nahum says the opposite. When the sun rises, the locusts "…fly away, and no one knows where." Nobody has a map for where they go.
Right. Nahum says, "When the sun rises, they fly away, and no one knows where." Nobody can say where they went. They're simply gone.
That's it. Nahum says to the king of Assyria, "Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them." Scattered, with nobody to bring them together. That's the king's problem.
Nahum says the opposite. The people are "…scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them." Nobody is doing any gathering in this verse.
Settled isn't the word, friend. Nahum says, "Your people are scattered on the mountains with no one to gather them." The word is scattered, and no one is gathering them.
Yes. Nahum says, "All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall…" Nobody in this verse is quiet about it. The news travels and the applause follows.
Weeping isn't what the verse says. Nahum says, "All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall…" The word is applaud.
Help isn't what the verse says. Nahum says, "All who hear the news of you applaud your downfall…" Applause is what the verse gives the news.

explanations.answer: They've all felt his constant cruelty
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Nahum gives. He says everyone applauds, "…for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?" He ends the whole book on that question. Everyone has felt it.

explanations.answer: They were all paid to cheer for it
explanations.explanation: Nobody gets a paycheck for cheering here. Nahum gives the reason himself: "…for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?" The applause comes from what people lived through.

explanations.answer: They never knew who he was
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Nahum says they applaud "…for who has not experienced your constant cruelty?" The reason he gives is what they experienced.
